blocks.content: This topic ties the module together with the practical payoff volumes exist for: real data, surviving real operations, that would otherwise destroy it.
1. Recreating a Container Without Losing Data
blocks.text: 1. Recreating a Container Without Losing Data

blocks.content: This is the everyday scenario volumes solve: you need to upgrade a database's image version, which means removing the old container and starting a new one. With the data directory mounted as a volume, the new container picks up exactly where the old one left off.

blocks.alt: A new container, the exact same data, uninterrupted

blocks.content: Mounting Postgres's actual data directory (/var/lib/postgresql/data) as a named volume means the database's tables, indexes, and rows live entirely independent of the container's own lifecycle, upgrading the Postgres image itself does not touch this data at all.

blocks.alt: The data directory itself, decoupled from the container

blocks.content:
docker run -d --name db-old -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15
docker rm -f db-old
docker run -d --name db-new -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
# db-new has exactly the same data db-old had.

code.content:
docker run -d --name db-old -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15
docker rm -f db-old
docker run -d --name db-new -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
# db-new has exactly the same data db-old had.

codes.bash:
docker run -d --name db-old -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:15
docker rm -f db-old
docker run -d --name db-new -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
# db-new has exactly the same data db-old had.

blocks.content: It is worth seeing the failure mode directly: run that same database container with no volume mounted at all, and every row of data lives only in the container's writable layer, one docker rm, accidental or intentional, and it is gone permanently, with no way to recover it.

blocks.alt: No volume means the data was never actually safe

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Volumes are what let you safely upgrade, restart, or recreate a stateful container without losing the data it holds.
Any container holding data you actually care about should have that data's directory mounted as a volume, without exception, the writable layer alone is not durable storage.
